key_terms.meaning: The data-link unit of transmission: a header, a payload and a trailer, with a visible start and end so the receiver can tell where one frame stops and the next begins.
The 8-bit delimiter 01111110 that marks the start and end of a frame.
The sender inserts a 0 after every five consecutive 1s in the payload, so the flag pattern can never appear inside the data; the receiver deletes that 0.
Parity bits added over every row and every column of a block of data; it detects a single-bit error and also points to its row and column.
Ones' complement sum of the 16-bit words of the data; the complement of the sum is sent, and the receiver's words plus checksum must sum to all 1s.
Cyclic redundancy check: the remainder of (data × 2^r) divided modulo 2 by a generator polynomial of degree r; those r bits travel with the frame.
The number of bit positions in which two valid codewords differ; a code with minimum distance d_min detects d_min − 1 errors and corrects ⌊(d_min − 1)/2⌋.
Redundant bits placed at positions 1, 2, 4, 8, …; check bit at position 2^i covers every data position whose index has bit i set, and the failed checks give the error position.
Flow-control rule where the sender may have up to W unacknowledged frames in flight; the window of allowed sequence numbers slides forward as ACKs arrive.
With n sequence bits there are 2^n numbers; Go-Back-N needs W ≤ 2^n − 1 and Selective Repeat needs W ≤ 2^(n−1) so ACKs are never ambiguous.
ARQ scheme where the receiver accepts only in-order frames and silently discards the rest; on a timeout or NAK the sender resends the lost frame and every frame after it.
ARQ scheme where the receiver buffers out-of-order frames and asks for only the missing one, so the sender retransmits just that frame.
An acknowledgement numbered n meaning every frame up to n − 1 has arrived; used by Go-Back-N and by TCP.
High-level Data Link Control: a bit-oriented protocol with flag-delimited frames, an 8- or 16-bit control field, and three frame types: information (I), supervisory (S) and unnumbered (U).
Point-to-Point Protocol: a byte-oriented link protocol with a fixed frame format, LCP for link setup, one NCP per network protocol, and a CRC but no retransmission.
Send whenever a frame is ready; throughput S = G·e^(−2G), maximum 1/(2e) ≈ 18.4% of the channel at G = 0.5.
After the nth collision, pick a random integer k from 0 to 2^n − 1 and wait k slot times before trying again.
Carrier sense multiple access with collision avoidance: sense the medium, wait DIFS, take a random backoff, transmit, and wait for an explicit ACK; RTS/CTS can reserve the medium.
Virtual LAN: a switch splits one physical LAN into separate broadcast domains, and frames on a trunk carry a 12-bit VLAN identifier in an 802.1Q tag.
Two stations that cannot hear each other but both reach the same access point, so carrier sense fails and their frames collide at the AP.

takeaways: A frame must carry its own start and end markers, and bit stuffing is what makes those markers unambiguous.
Every detection scheme trades redundancy for certainty: parity catches odd numbers of errors, checksums catch most random errors cheaply, and CRC catches burst errors with a polynomial remainder.
Hamming codes turn redundancy into repair, not just alarm, because well-placed check bits spell out the position of a single flipped bit.
Flow control protects the receiver's buffer; a sliding window lets the sender keep the link full while still staying inside that buffer.
ARQ adds a timer and acknowledgements, so Go-Back-N trades bandwidth for simple receiver logic while Selective Repeat trades receiver memory for bandwidth.
HDLC shows the bit-oriented shape of a link protocol and PPP shows the byte-oriented shape; PPP skips error control and leaves reliability to higher layers.
When many stations share one medium, the MAC rule decides who talks: ALOHA talks at will, CSMA listens first, and CSMA/CD both listens and detects collisions.
Ethernet fixes the frame format and addressing for wired LANs, and VLANs let one switch carry many separate broadcast domains.
Radio makes carrier sense unreliable, so 802.11 uses CSMA/CA with ACKs, priority gaps, backoff and optional RTS/CTS instead of collision detection.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are mostly numeric work on CRC, checksums and Hamming codes plus comparison questions on ARQ schemes, HDLC versus PPP, and the ALOHA/CSMA family, so practise the calculations and keep a comparison table ready.

bank.q: Why does a data-link frame need explicit delimiters? Explain bit stuffing for the flag 01111110 with a short example, and explain byte stuffing as an alternative.
outline: Frames arrive back to back on a bit stream, so the receiver needs a fixed pattern to find frame boundaries.
The flag 01111110 marks start and end; the same pattern must never occur inside the payload.
Sender: after five consecutive 1s in the data, insert a 0; receiver deletes a 0 that follows five 1s.
Byte stuffing: escape the flag byte with a special ESC byte in byte-oriented protocols.
Stuffed bits depend on the data, so the receiver must unstuff before passing the payload up.

bank.q: Compare single parity, two-dimensional parity, the Internet checksum and CRC: what each computes, what error patterns each misses, and what it costs.
outline: Single parity: one bit makes the count of 1s even; detects any odd number of errors, misses any even number.
Two-dimensional parity: parity over rows and columns of a block; detects and localises a single-bit error, misses many multi-bit patterns.
Checksum: ones' complement 16-bit sum, sent complemented; receiver's total must be all 1s; weak against some reorderings.
CRC: modulo-2 remainder against a generator polynomial of degree r; catches all single-bit errors, all bursts of length ≤ r, and all odd numbers of errors if the generator has the factor (x + 1).
Cost grows from one bit to r bits; CRC needs shift-register hardware but is cheap in practice.

bank.q: Explain how a Hamming code corrects a single-bit error: how the number of check bits is chosen, where they are placed, and how the receiver finds the bad bit.
outline: If m data bits need r check bits, the condition is 2^r ≥ m + r + 1, so the r failed/passed checks can name m + r positions plus the no-error case.
Check bits sit at positions 1, 2, 4, 8, … and data occupies the remaining positions.
Each check bit is the parity of all positions whose index contains that power of two.
Receiver recomputes the checks; the failed checks, read as a binary number, give the position of the flipped bit.
Flipping that bit repairs the frame, which is why correction costs more redundancy than detection.

bank.q: Explain stop-and-wait flow control and the sliding window protocol. Why does a window of W frames use a link better than one frame at a time?
outline: Stop-and-wait: send one frame, stop, wait for the ACK, then send the next; the link idles for one round trip after each frame.
A sliding window lets the sender keep up to W frames unacknowledged; the window covers sequence numbers from the oldest unacknowledged frame to that number plus W − 1.
ACKs slide the window forward, so the sender never overruns the receiver's buffer.
Utilisation for stop-and-wait is 1/(1 + 2a) with a = propagation delay / transmission time; a window of W raises it to about W/(1 + 2a) until the link is full.
Pacing is the point: the window size is the receiver's promise about how much it can hold.

bank.q: Compare the frame formats of HDLC and PPP, and explain what LCP and NCP do in PPP.
outline: HDLC: flag, address, control, information, FCS, flag; bit-oriented, so bit stuffing applies.
HDLC control field is 8 or 16 bits; three frame types: I (data), S (supervisory, carries ACK/NAK and window control), U (unnumbered, link setup and teardown).
PPP: flag 01111110, address 11111111, control 00000011, protocol, payload, FCS, flag; byte-oriented, so byte stuffing with the escape byte 01111101 applies.
LCP sets up, tests and closes the link, and negotiates options such as authentication and maximum receive unit.
NCP, one per network-layer protocol, configures that protocol on the link; PPP itself has no sequence numbers and no retransmission.

bank.q: Using the generator polynomial x³ + 1 (bit pattern 1001) and the 6-bit data 101110, compute the CRC and write the transmitted frame.
outline: Degree of the generator is 3, so append three zeros: dividend is 101110000.
Divide modulo 2, XORing the generator whenever the leading bit is 1.
The 3-bit remainder here is 011.
Transmitted frame = data followed by remainder = 101110011.
Receiver divides the whole received frame by 1001; a zero remainder means no detected error.

bank.q: A 4-bit data block 1011 is to be sent with a Hamming code. Find the number of check bits, place them, compute them, and give the transmitted codeword.
outline: With m = 4, 2^r ≥ 4 + r + 1 gives r = 3, so the codeword is 7 bits, a (7,4) code.
Check bits go at positions 1, 2, 4; data bits at 3, 5, 6, 7.
Write the three parity equations: position 1 covers 1, 3, 5, 7; position 2 covers 2, 3, 6, 7; position 4 covers 4, 5, 6, 7.
Substitute the data bits and solve for each check bit.
State the 7-bit codeword and show the receiver's check giving 000 for no error.

bank.q: A link runs at 1 Mbps with 1000-bit frames and a one-way propagation delay of 20 ms. Find the utilisation of stop-and-wait, and the smallest window that keeps the link 100% busy.
outline: Transmission time t_f = 1000 bits / 1 Mbps = 1 ms.
Round trip = 2 × 20 ms = 40 ms; a = 40/2 = 20 relative to transmission time.
Stop-and-wait utilisation = 1/(1 + 40) ≈ 2.4%.
Full utilisation needs the sender busy for 41 ms per round trip, so W ≈ 41 frames.
Round up to the next power-of-two-friendly value and check the sequence-number bound for the chosen ARQ scheme.

bank.q: A pure ALOHA system has 1000-bit frames on a 1 Mbps channel. Compute the throughput at G = 0.5 and the maximum throughput the system can reach, in frames per second.
outline: Frame time t_f = 1000/1 Mbps = 1 ms, so the channel offers 1000 frames per second at full load.
Pure ALOHA throughput S = G·e^(−2G); at G = 0.5, e^(−1) ≈ 0.368, so S ≈ 0.184.
Maximum is at G = 0.5, giving 1/(2e) ≈ 18.4% of 1000 frames per second, about 184 frames per second.
Compare with slotted ALOHA, whose maximum is 1/e ≈ 36.8%, because vulnerable time halves from 2t_f to t_f.
State that both figures assume Poisson arrivals and no capture effect.

bank.q: Analyse why collision detection does not work on a radio LAN, and explain how IEEE 802.11 CSMA/CA with DIFS/SIFS and RTS/CTS makes up for it.
outline: A radio transmitter cannot hear a collision at its own antenna, so CSMA/CD's detection step is impossible; there is also the hidden terminal problem.
Carrier sense is unreliable because of fading, distance and asymmetric links, so two stations may both think the medium is free.
CSMA/CA avoids rather than detects: sense, wait DIFS if idle, take a random backoff, transmit and wait for a link-layer ACK.
SIFS is shorter than DIFS, so ACKs and CTS go out before anyone else can contend; the duration field sets each station's NAV timer.
RTS/CTS reserves the medium around the receiver and silences hidden terminals; binary exponential backoff spreads out stations after collisions.

bank.q: A factory wants a shared network for control traffic with hard deadlines. Compare random access, controlled access and channelisation, and recommend one with reasons.
outline: Random access (ALOHA, CSMA, CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA) has no central control and gives good throughput at light load, but delay is unbounded and collisions are possible at any time.
Controlled access (polling, token passing) gives every station a guaranteed turn and bounded delay, at the cost of a central point or token overhead.
Channelisation (FDMA, TDMA, CDMA) gives dedicated capacity with no contention, but wastes capacity when a station is idle.
Hard deadlines rule out random access; token passing or a scheduled TDMA slot fits best, and a token ring or a scheduled industrial Ethernet variant is the practical choice.
State the trade-off in one line: guarantees cost capacity, and random access spends capacity to buy simplicity.

bank.q: Explain why Go-Back-N needs W ≤ 2^n − 1 and Selective Repeat needs W ≤ 2^(n−1). Show what goes wrong when the bound is crossed.
outline: n sequence bits give 2^n distinct numbers, and the receiver must never confuse a new frame with an old one that was retransmitted.
In Go-Back-N the receiver accepts only in order and holds no buffer, so a window equal to 2^n makes a retransmitted frame look like the next new frame.
In Selective Repeat the receiver buffers up to W frames, so W and 2^n − W must not overlap: 2W ≤ 2^n, giving W ≤ 2^(n−1).
Give a small worked case, such as n = 3 with W = 8 versus W = 4, and trace the duplicate.
Conclude that the bound is set by the receiver's buffer and by ACK ambiguity, and that the cost of a larger window is more sequence bits or more buffering.

bank.q: Design the link layer for a campus with three buildings: wired Ethernet between switches, an 802.1Q trunk to the core, and Wi-Fi access points on each floor. Justify the broadcast-domain and MAC choices.
outline: Ethernet 802.3 fixes the frame format, the 48-bit MAC address and the 64-byte minimum frame; the 4-byte FCS guards each frame.
Keep one VLAN per department or per floor so broadcast traffic and ARP storms stay local; the 12-bit 802.1Q tag on the trunk keeps the domains separate over shared links.
CSMA/CD governs the shared half-duplex segment; on switched full-duplex links it is effectively off, so the 5-4-3 rule matters only for legacy shared segments.
Wi-Fi cannot use CSMA/CD, so each AP runs CSMA/CA with its own BSS, SSID and ACKs; the AP is the bridge between the wireless and wired broadcast domains.
Evaluate: VLANs give isolation and policy control at the cost of configuration and inter-VLAN routing; wireless adds contention and retransmission that wired users do not see.

glossary.def: A data-link layer protocol data unit, made of a header, a payload and a trailer carrying the start and end markers.
Inserting one 0 after every five consecutive 1s in the data so the flag pattern cannot appear inside a frame.
Inserting an escape byte in front of any byte in the payload that happens to equal the flag or the escape byte.
Parity computed over both the rows and the columns of a block of bits, which detects any single-bit error and locates it.
A ones' complement sum of 16-bit words, sent in complemented form, that the receiver re-adds to check the data.
A cyclic redundancy check, computed as the modulo-2 remainder of the data shifted left by r bits, divided by a generator polynomial of degree r.
The fixed bit pattern of degree r that both sender and receiver divide by when computing a CRC.
A block code with check bits at power-of-two positions, able to correct any single-bit error.
The count of positions in which two codewords differ; the minimum over all pairs sets how many errors a code can detect or correct.
Flow control that sends one frame and waits for its acknowledgement before sending the next.
A flow-control scheme where the sender keeps up to W unacknowledged frames in flight and advances the window as ACKs arrive.
Automatic Repeat reQuest: error control that pairs acknowledgements with a retransmission timer so lost or damaged frames are sent again.
An ARQ scheme where the receiver discards out-of-order frames and the sender resends the missing frame and everything after it.
An ARQ scheme where the receiver buffers out-of-order frames and the sender resends only the frame that was lost.
A negative acknowledgement telling the sender that a specific frame arrived damaged or never arrived.
Carrying the acknowledgement for the other direction inside the data frame travelling in this direction, instead of sending a separate ACK.
A bit-oriented data link protocol with flag-delimited frames, a control field and three frame classes: information, supervisory and unnumbered.
A byte-oriented point-to-point protocol with a fixed frame format, LCP link negotiation, per-protocol NCPs and a frame check sequence.
A random access scheme in which a station transmits whenever it has a frame, with no sensing of the channel.
Random access in which stations may transmit only at the start of a time slot, halving the vulnerable period and doubling peak throughput to 1/e.
Carrier sense multiple access with collision detection: listen before sending, keep listening while sending, and stop and back off as soon as a collision is heard.
Carrier sense multiple access with collision avoidance: sense, wait a priority gap, back off randomly, transmit, and rely on an explicit acknowledgement.
Choosing a random wait of 0 to 2^n − 1 slot times after the nth collision, so contention thins out quickly.
A logical LAN created inside a switch, forming its own broadcast domain; frames on a trunk carry a 12-bit VLAN identifier.
Basic Service Set: one IEEE 802.11 cell, identified by an SSID and served by one access point.
A station that can reach the access point but not the other stations, so carrier sense does not warn it about an ongoing transmission.
